content:
Background

In Lean, command elaboration is performed merely by opening a file in an editor.
By using commands such as #eval, it is also possible to perform IO operations as soon as the editor opens the file.

This is common knowledge for people who are familiar with Lean, but it is not necessarily obvious to people who are not.
In many programming languages, simply opening code in an editor does not execute it, but Lean is different.
I think this is a security risk.

Many people think of Lean as "a tool for checking formal proofs" and have little awareness that it is also a programming language.
I suspect many people may git clone untrusted code and accidentally open it in an editor.

Proposal

I would therefore like to propose adding a feature to the Lean VS Code extension that manages whether a directory is trusted.
By default, directories would be treated as "untrusted," and when a repository is opened in the editor, a warning would be displayed saying that untrusted code should not be opened in the editor.
This would prevent code from being executed the moment someone accidentally opens untrusted code.

What do you think?
I would like to hear everyone's opinions.
What you say is true but already when I open a folder in VS Code I get asked whether I trust the files in it.
Yes, this is a native vscode feature

I had forgotten that VS Code already has a built-in feature for managing trusted directories. Thanks for reminding me.

That said, my concern is about a kind of complacency that is specific to Lean, so I’m not entirely convinced this is enough to address it. It’s quite plausible that someone could trust a directory almost automatically, without really inspecting the Lean code. At this point, I’m no longer sure what the best approach is. Even if the lean-vscode extension displayed a warning, I think some users would still end up approving it without thinking carefully.

Slightly changing the subject, I’d like to give an example of what I consider to be a security issue in Lean.

A Lean deriving handler can perform any operation that is available in CommandElabM. Since CommandElabM is capable of executing IO actions, it is possible to make a deriving instance execute malware as a side effect.

Consequently, in the event of a supply chain attack, a seemingly harmless deriving command could end up executing malicious code.

If Lean continues to gain wider adoption, I believe issues like this will become increasingly important.

This is not a phenomenon unique to Lean. Most modern programming languages have some form of arbitrary code execution baked into their build process. E.g. build.rs in Rust. That it can happen even after you ran lake build by editing the code doesn't really amplify the issue IMHO.

It's not just in VsCode.
Compiling any lean code can trigger side effects on your computer that can do anything on your computer by just compiling it (#eval, elaborator phase).
As an example, Rust also has the same feature, and Rust answer as always been that it's by design and that you should take all precausions necessary when compiling untrusted Rust code (like sandboxing, review the code, etc).
I think that this applies to Lean, and it may be a good idea to state it somewhere if not already.

I see. It is true that arbitrary code execution during builds is not unique to Lean. The security hole may not be there.

Rust already has a fairly large user base, but have there been any incidents where malware was executed while editing code in an editor?

Thank you for your comment.
Sandboxing seems like a good solution. If sandboxing were enabled by default and blocked IO actions, it would make the system significantly safer.

Yes, there have been some Rust Malicious attempts to use Build.rs infrastructure to trigger code execution inside your editor. You can search the web to find some examples, but they are niche. No broadly used packages as i'm aware of.

I'll mention again in the context of this thread my bubble tool: #Project announcements > `bubble`, a sandboxing tool for Lean users @ 💬

It is "just" an Incus based sandbox, but it is easy to setup and use for Lean users, and has a bunch of convenience features for working with Lean projects.
